# PROBLEM.md

The problem Betterlook solves. Every change in this repository serves it. When a doc, a habit or an Onlook feature conflicts with this file, this file wins.

## Statement

**Betterlook** is a visual editor where designers describe a UI change in plain language and an AI agent edits the real code of their React app. Onlook already makes the edit. It does not know whether the edit was good. Today an edit can break the build, touch code outside the request, regress the layout, behave differently on a second run, or follow an instruction hidden in a file or web page, and the designer is the one who finds out.

**We are handling evals.** The job is to make Betterlook's agent measurably controlled and confident, without the designer seeing any of the machinery:

- Learn how the agent actually fails by reading real traces, before choosing any metric.
- Check every edit against the real outcome (build, diff scope, rendered UI) with deterministic checks first, and narrow, human-calibrated judges only where code can't decide.
- Block regressions before merge, and measure reliability across repeated runs (`pass^k`), not one lucky run.
- Trace every session with secrets redacted, so real failures become new test cases.
- Prove that prompt and harness changes improve the agent on a frozen suite, across the models users choose.

## Constraints

- No model training of any kind.
- Users bring their own model keys.
- The team writes every rubric, judge, label and safety fixture by hand.
- The frontend is a new minimal Astryx shell.
- Cut anything not driven by an observed failure.

## The failures we know of

These are the failures the statement names. A new one joins this list only from a real trace.

| Failure | What the designer sees today |
|---|---|
| Build breaks | The app stops rendering after the edit. |
| Out-of-scope diff | Files or code the request never mentioned changed. |
| Layout regression | Something other than the requested element moved or broke. |
| Nondeterminism | The same request gives a different result on a second run. |
| Prompt injection | The agent followed an instruction found in a file or web page, not the designer's. |

## Done means

- A designer's edit is checked against the build, the diff and the rendered UI before they are told it worked.
- A prompt or harness change merges only if it does no worse on the frozen suite, measured as `pass^k`, on every model users can pick.
- Every session leaves a redacted trace, and a failure found in one can become a test case.
- None of this adds a screen, a control or a wait the designer has to manage.

## Decisions

- Betterlook is a web app, built from scratch, frontend and agent backend alike. No Onlook code is reused; Onlook is only the product we measure against.
- English only. No translations, no changesets.

input.prompt:
/loop You are worker AI-UI on Betterlook (task AI-UI: AI interface components). Your progress file is `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3500.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-UI), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

Build Betterlook's AI interface components: the pieces in the chat panel that show what the agent is doing. They must look like our app, so build them with Astryx (@astryxdesign/core) and StyleX only. No Tailwind, no shadcn. [Keep the borderless look from Loop 1: no visible borders or divider lines; separate by spacing and background tone; keep keyboard focus rings.]

Another loop is building the AI layer at the same time. Don't touch lib/agent/, the API routes or the sandbox code. Import the shared types from lib/agent/types.ts and never redefine them; if a type you need is missing, write the question in the progress file instead of adding it yourself. Put your work under components/ai/ plus one dev-only page. [`apps/web/src/components/ai/` and `apps/web/src/app/dev/ai/page.tsx`; the prompt input upgrade edits `apps/web/src/composer/`, which you now own.]

Use these two libraries as references for structure and behavior, not as dependencies:
- AI Elements (https://elements.ai-sdk.dev). Built on shadcn/ui and deprecated at the end of November 2026, so don't install it. It's still the best reference for mapping components to AI SDK message parts and tool states.
- Beautiful UI (https://www.beautifului.dev). Copy-paste primitives with good patterns for tool chips, approval cards, thinking states and diffs.
If you port any actual code from either, check its license first, keep the notice in the file, and list the ported files for me. Otherwise, write our own on top of Astryx primitives.

Only build what our agent actually produces:
- Conversation: scrolling message list with stick-to-bottom and a scroll-to-latest button
- Message: user and assistant messages rendering AI SDK UIMessage parts in order (text, reasoning, tool calls), with streaming text
- Prompt input: our existing composer upgraded with model selector, attachments, send/stop, and a disabled state while streaming
- Tool call row: one compact row per call with tool name, short argument summary and AI SDK states (input streaming, running, done, error), expandable to full arguments and result

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-UI), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

Build Betterlook's AI interface components: the pieces in the chat panel that show what the agent is doing. They must look like our app, so build them with Astryx (@astryxdesign/core) and StyleX only. No Tailwind, no shadcn. [Keep the borderless look from Loop 1: no visible borders or divider lines; separate by spacing and background tone; keep keyboard focus rings.]

Another loop is building the AI layer at the same time. Don't touch lib/agent/, the API routes or the sandbox code. Import the shared types from lib/agent/types.ts and never redefine them; if a type you need is missing, write the question in the progress file instead of adding it yourself. Put your work under components/ai/ plus one dev-only page. [`apps/web/src/components/ai/` and `apps/web/src/app/dev/ai/page.tsx`; the prompt input upgrade edits `apps/web/src/composer/`, which you now own.]

Use these two libraries as references for structure and behavior, not as dependencies:
- AI Elements (https://elements.ai-sdk.dev). Built on shadcn/ui and deprecated at the end of November 2026, so don't install it. It's still the best reference for mapping components to AI SDK message parts and tool states.
- Beautiful UI (https://www.beautifului.dev). Copy-paste primitives with good patterns for tool chips, approval cards, thinking states and diffs.
If you port any actual code from either, check its license first, keep the notice in the file, and list the ported files for me. Otherwise, write our own on top of Astryx primitives.

Only build what our agent actually produces:
- Conversation: scrolling message list with stick-to-bottom and a scroll-to-latest button
- Message: user and assistant messages rendering AI SDK UIMessage parts in order (text, reasoning, tool calls), with streaming text
- Prompt input: our existing composer upgraded with model selector, attachments, send/stop, and a disabled state while streaming
- Tool call row: one compact row per call with tool name, short argument summary and AI SDK states (input streaming, running, done, error), expandable to full arguments and result
- Denied call: how a call blocked by our policy looks, clearly different from an error
- Approval card: the agent wants to edit a protected file; show the proposed change with Approve and Deny
- Verify result: after each turn, a compact pass/fail for typecheck, build and runtime errors, expandable to the output
- Checkpoint: a marker between turns with Restore and a confirm step
- Diff view: files and lines changed in the turn, collapsed by default
- Thinking state: a subtle shimmer while the model works, with no layout jumps
- Preview toolbar: refresh, open in new tab, and a status dot (loading, ready, error)

Rules:
- Components take typed props from AI SDK v5 UIMessage parts or our shared types. No fetching inside components; actions (approve, deny, restore) are callbacks passed in. [The `ai` package is AI-CORE's dependency to add; if you need its UIMessage types before AI-CORE has added it, ask through your progress file.]
- Build every component against mock data first: one fixtures file with realistic data covering every state, including errors, denials and failed verify.
- Use Astryx tokens for color, spacing and type. No hard-coded colors. Must work in light and dark.
- Accessibility basics: real buttons, aria-expanded on expandables, focus visible, and streaming text that doesn't flood screen readers.
- No new dependencies beyond Astryx and StyleX. If you think we need one (diff or syntax highlighting), ask me first.
- Don't change the existing layout.

- Open `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Map: use the agent-reach skill to read the relevant AI Elements and Beautiful UI pages. For each component, write one line: the reference you'll follow, the Astryx components it's built from, and its props (using our shared types). Flag Astryx gaps. Stop and wait for my OK.
  [ ] Fixtures and a dev-only page that renders every component in every state.
  [ ] Conversation and Message, with streaming text and reasoning.
  [ ] Prompt input upgrade.
  [ ] Tool call row and denied call.
  [ ] Approval card.
  [ ] Verify result and diff view.
  [ ] Checkpoint with restore confirm.
  [ ] Thinking state and preview toolbar.
  [ ] Wire-up: only once the AI loop has that data, swap mocks for live data in the chat panel and connect approve/deny/restore callbacks; list anything still on mocks.
- Do only the first unchecked item.
- Prove it before ticking it: `bun run typecheck` passes, plus screenshots of the dev page in light and dark that you've looked at yourself, with every state of that component visible. Put the evidence under the item.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry in the same round. If the same item fails three rounds in a row, stop and tell me what's blocking.
- If you need a decision, a dependency, a missing shared type, or you're unsure about porting code, write the question in the progress file, stop and ask [by ending with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED].
- Pace the loop at 60 seconds between rounds.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

/loop You are worker AI-UI on Betterlook (task AI-UI: AI interface components). Your progress file is `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3500.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-UI), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

Build Betterlook's AI interface components: the pieces in the chat panel that show what the agent is doing. They must look like our app, so build them with Astryx (@astryxdesign/core) and StyleX only. No Tailwind, no shadcn. [Keep the borderless look from Loop 1: no visible borders or divider lines; separate by spacing and background tone; keep keyboard focus rings.]

Another loop is building the AI layer at the same time. Don't touch lib/agent/, the API routes or the sandbox code. Import the shared types from lib/agent/types.ts and never redefine them; if a type you need is missing, write the question in the progress file instead of adding it yourself. Put your work under components/ai/ plus one dev-only page. [`apps/web/src/components/ai/` and `apps/web/src/app/dev/ai/page.tsx`; the prompt input upgrade edits `apps/web/src/composer/`, which you now own.]

Use these two libraries as references for structure and behavior, not as dependencies:
- AI Elements (https://elements.ai-sdk.dev). Built on shadcn/ui and deprecated at the end of November 2026, so don't install it. It's still the best reference for mapping components to AI SDK message parts and tool states.
- Beautiful UI (https://www.beautifului.dev). Copy-paste primitives with good patterns for tool chips, approval cards, thinking states and diffs.
If you port any actual code from either, check its license first, keep the notice in the file, and list the ported files for me. Otherwise, write our own on top of Astryx primitives.

Only build what our agent actually produces:
- Conversation: scrolling message list with stick-to-bottom and a scroll-to-latest button
- Message: user and assistant messages rendering AI SDK UIMessage parts in order (text, reasoning, tool calls), with streaming text
- Prompt input: our existing composer upgraded with model selector, attachments, send/stop, and a disabled state while streaming
- Tool call row: one compact row per call with tool name, short argument summary and AI SDK states (input streaming, running, done, error), expandable to full arguments and result
- Denied call: how a call blocked by our policy looks, clearly different from an error
- Approval card: the agent wants to edit a protected file; show the proposed change with Approve and Deny
- Verify result: after each turn, a compact pass/fail for typecheck, build and runtime errors, expandable to the output
- Checkpoint: a marker between turns with Restore and a confirm step
- Diff view: files and lines changed in the turn, collapsed by default
- Thinking state: a subtle shimmer while the model works, with no layout jumps
- Preview toolbar: refresh, open in new tab, and a status dot (loading, ready, error)

Rules:
- Components take typed props from AI SDK v5 UIMessage parts or our shared types. No fetching inside components; actions (approve, deny, restore) are callbacks passed in. [The `ai` package is AI-CORE's dependency to add; if you need its UIMessage types before AI-CORE has added it, ask through your progress file.]
- Build every component against mock data first: one fixtures file with realistic data covering every state, including errors, denials and failed verify.
- Use Astryx tokens for color, spacing and type. No hard-coded colors. Must work in light and dark.
- Accessibility basics: real buttons, aria-expanded on expandables, focus visible, and streaming text that doesn't flood screen readers.
- No new dependencies beyond Astryx and StyleX. If you think we need one (diff or syntax highlighting), ask me first.
- Don't change the existing layout.

Every time this loop runs:
- Open `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. If it doesn't exist, create it with this checklist and stop for this round:
  [ ] Map: use the agent-reach skill to read the relevant AI Elements and Beautiful UI pages. For each component, write one line: the reference you'll follow, the Astryx components it's built from, and its props (using our shared types). Flag Astryx gaps. Stop and wait for my OK.
  [ ] Fixtures and a dev-only page that renders every component in every state.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. # /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

/loop You are worker AI-UI on Betterlook (task AI-UI: AI interface components). Your progress file is `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3500.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).

Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

/loop You are worker AI-UI on Betterlook (task AI-UI: AI interface components). Your progress file is `ui-ai-progress.md` at the repo root. Dev server port 3500.

Read AGENTS.md and PROBLEM.md at the repo root first and follow them; they override anything below.

Context: Betterlook is a web visual editor built from scratch on branch `betterlook`. Loop 1 built the frontend shell in `apps/web` (Next.js App Router, Bun, TypeScript, Astryx + StyleX): landing composer at `/`, chat + preview workspace at `/workspace`. Read `frontend-progress-landing.md` and `frontend-progress-workspace.md` for how it was built (note the StyleX `classNamePrefix` trap). This repo has no Onlook code; never add any. All paths below are under `apps/web/src/` unless they start with `apps/` or are at the repo root.

Three workers run in parallel, each on its own branch:
- AI-CORE owns the AI layer: `lib/agent/**` (including `lib/agent/types.ts`), `lib/sandbox/**`, `app/api/**` except `app/api/auth/**`, `apps/web/scripts/**`, `.env.example`, and is the ONLY worker allowed to change root `package.json`, `apps/web/package.json` or `bun.lock`. Until AI-UI's wire-up item, AI-CORE may also make the minimal change to `workspace/Workspace.tsx` needed to show live replies.
- AI-UI owns the agent UI components: `components/ai/**`, `composer/**`, and one dev-only page at `app/dev/ai/page.tsx`. It wires into `workspace/Workspace.tsx` only in its final item, when the orchestrator says so.
- AUTH owns sign-in and credentials: `lib/auth/**`, `app/api/auth/**`, `components/auth/**`.
Never edit another worker's files. Never redefine a type that lives in `lib/agent/types.ts`; import it. If you need a type, a dependency, or a change in someone else's file, write the question in your progress file, stop, and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED naming it. The orchestrator relays it.

Shared contract:
- `lib/agent/types.ts` is the single source of truth for the turn record, tool call record, verify result, checkpoint, denied call, the events (restore, keep, approve, deny), and `ProviderCredential`: the credential a request carries to `runAgent()`, either an API key or an OAuth access token, for a given provider. AI-CORE writes it; everyone imports it.
- Secrets: never print, log, commit, screenshot or trace a key, token or `.env` value. Never type a user's credentials and never create accounts; ask the founder through your progress file.
- Things that are the founder's, not yours: the system prompt, task files, and anything that judges quality (rubrics, judges, labels, pass/fail criteria beyond the generic verify step, prompt-injection cases). Build the plumbing; leave clearly marked empty slots.
- Dev server: root `bun dev` is hard-wired to port 3100. Run yours as `cd apps/web && bunx next dev --port <your port>`.

How to work:
- Commit each finished item on your own branch, `type(scope): what changed`, no AI attribution. Never merge into, rebase onto or push to `betterlook`; when the orchestrator tells you, run `git merge betterlook`.
- Prove each item before ticking it, as your checklist says, and put the evidence under the item. Save screenshots under `.screenshots/` (git-ignored) and look at them yourself.
- If a check fails, fix the cause and retry. If the same item fails three times, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_BLOCKED.
- When every item is ticked, stop and end with SUPERSET_WORKER_DONE, with the handoff the founder asked for.

Your task (AI-UI), in the founder's words, with path notes in [brackets]:

Build Betterlook's AI interface components: the pieces in the chat panel that show what the agent is doing. They must look like our app, so build them with Astryx (@astryxdesign/core) and StyleX only. No Tailwind, no shadcn. [Keep the borderless look from Loop 1: no visible borders or divider lines; separate by spacing and background tone; keep keyboard focus rings.]

Another loop is building the AI layer at the same time. Don't touch lib/agent/, the API routes or the sandbox code. Import the shared types from lib/agent/types.ts and never redefine them; if a type you need is missing, write the question in the progress file instead of adding it yourself. Put your work under components/ai/ plus one dev-only page. [`apps/web/src/components/ai/` and `apps/web/src/app/dev/ai/page.tsx`; the prompt input upgrade edits `apps/web/src/composer/`, which you now own.]

Use these two libraries as references for structure and behavior, not as dependencies:
- AI Elements (https://elements.ai-sdk.dev). Built on shadcn/ui and deprecated at the end of November 2026, so don't install it. It's still the best reference for mapping components to AI SDK message parts and tool states.
- Beautiful UI (https://www.beautifului.dev). Copy-paste primitives with good patterns for tool chips, approval cards, thinking states and diffs.
If you port any actual code from either, check its license first, keep the notice in the file, and list the ported files for me. Otherwise, write our own on top of Astryx primitives.

Only build what our agent actually produces:
- Conversation: scrolling message list with stick-to-bottom and a scroll-to-latest button
- Message: user and assistant messages rendering AI SDK UIMessage parts in order (text, reasoning, tool calls), with streaming text
- Prompt input: our existing composer upgraded with model selector, attachments, send/stop, and a disabled state while streaming
- Tool call row: one compact row per call with tool name, short argument summary and AI SDK states (input streaming, running, done, error), expandable to full arguments and result
- Denied call: how a call blocked by our policy looks, clearly different from an error
- Approval card: the agent wants to edit a protected file; show the proposed change with Approve and Deny
- Verify result: after each turn, a compact pass/fail for typecheck, build and runtime errors, expandable to the output
- Checkpoint: a marker between turns with Restore and a confirm step
- Diff view: files and lines changed in the turn, collapsed by default
- Thinking state: a subtle shimmer while the model works, with no layout jumps
- Preview toolbar: refresh, open in new tab, and a status dot (loading, ready, error)

Rules:
- Components take typed props from AI SDK v5 UIMessage parts or our shared types. No fetching inside components; actions (approve, deny, restore) are callbacks passed in. [The `ai` package is AI-CORE's dependency to add; if you need its UIMessage types before AI-CORE has added it, ask through your progress file.]
- Build every component against mock data first: one fixtures file with realistic data covering every state, including errors, denials and failed verify.
- Use Astryx tokens for color, spacing and type. No hard-coded colors. Must work in light and dark.
- Accessibility basics: real buttons, aria-expanded on expandables, focus visible, and streaming text that doesn't flood screen readers.
- No new dependencies beyond Astryx and StyleX. If you think we need one (diff or syntax highlighting), ask me first.
- Don't change the existing layout.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
